p: And who’s responding to the press in this office? I assume it’s you, because you said that you were the only member of the office currently?
No, there are two of us like I said.
Oh, okay. I apologize.
And we have a comms team in City Hall.

Okay. Could you send us some of the statements that you’ve made condemning antisemitic incidents? We would appreciate that, because I haven’t seen anything, and we did a Google search like my colleague mentioned. We didn’t find anything from the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism.
Sure. I’ll have our comms office pull that.

Do you plan to release any reports on the work that you’re doing,

and if so, could you just tell us what kind of reports?

Sure. So, as I indicated before, we’re doing a listening at the beginning of our work in this administration, and the first thing we’ll be producing is a public-facing document reporting on what we learned from that, and then also plan to be publishing something that is like the antisemitism strategy. I think we had planned to in this first iteration do so including suggestions for investments, policy and programming, but because of where we are in the budget cycle, that won’t be right away after we conduct this listening tour, but we do plan to produce a report following that and then I imagine over the next four years additional reports as we learn what’s needed.
Thank you. And have you reached out to any of the District Attorneys to discuss antisemitic hate crimes or antisemitism in general or your work?
So far, this office has a relationship with DA Bragg’s office, but do plan to reach out to other District Attorneys for sure.

Okay. The 2025 Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism report recommended capital funding for physical security to protect against vehicle attacks and others at vulnerable Jewish institutions. Can you confirm if this specific infrastructure funding is prioritized and fully accounted for in the Mayor’s upcoming Executive Capital Budget?

I can’t yet speak to the outcomes of the Executive Budget conversations, but I know that we are having conversations, but I know that we are having conversations about hard security including things like bollards.
Yeah, that’s exactly what I’m actually talking about. So, is that something that this office supports?
We’re in discussion about it.

Okay. Could you let us know what– thank you. Are you aware of the incident– the incident I discussed earlier with the NYPD, the incident that took place in my district where protestors marched down a street past a

synagogue and a daycare center and chanted and intimidated worshipers and children and their parents, and as a result parents don’t feel that their children are safe? Are you aware of this incident?
I’m aware of the incident, yeah.
And when did you become aware of it?
I believe yesterday or the day before, early this week.

So, in situations like this, could you tell us a little bit about what the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism does? You know, do they condemn it? How do they– what do they do after incidents like this take place?

So, in some incidents like this where there’s been something that was traumatizing to a community, we’ve gone and met with those who are impacted when– example of this is an Israeli kosher restaurant on the Upper East Side. after there was an incident there, we went and talked about what they needed and offered support, made sure to connect them with the NYPD. In fact, called and

sort of tried to ensure a speedy response from the NYPD. Some of this is about what we know. So, as we build this office and our infrastructure and our reporting relationships with other agencies, I expect we will be sort of fine tuning this reporting in and our relationship to incidents that happen. But it is definitely our intention to build relationships with anyone who is impacted by something scary that happens to them.
And then once you talk to these individuals and victims, and by the way, we welcome you in our district, and I don’t know if you reached out to any of the parents or the community.
No, not yet, but I welcome being connected.
Okay. What is it that you would do after that, following speaking to victims? Like, would you advocate for the NYPD to prosecute or like what is it that– what action do you take after that?

So, the NYPD’s processes are certainly their own, but if they haven’t yet reported, we would recommend that they

report either to NYPD if there’s something criminal, if there’s discrimination to CCHR. We talk to all of our colleagues about what the best government approach is, but sometimes as we’ve heard here, there are things that are upsetting and traumatizing that don’t rise to the level of crime, and in that case, it’s talking through connecting to community supports, keeping in touch about prevention of future incidents, that sort of thing.
Okay. Thank you. And we look forward to working with you and being in touch.
You too. Thank you.
Council Member Brewer?

Thank you very much. For Mr. Gerber, on the west side, as you can imagine, the 24 is helpful, the 20, Sunset [sic] Park, certainly Midtown north and certainly the DA’s Office, and we do get way too many paint on Jewish restaurants. We get tons of of swastikas on benches in the park and graffiti, way too much of it that’s antisemitic. But two issues– there is confusion.

Obviously, if it’s a violent crime we’re going to call 911 on any topic. But there is some confusion about whether people call 311 or they call 911, and we tell people because we’ve had so many, stay on the site, don’t leave until NYPD arrives, no matter what you call. NYPD takes a report, takes photographs, and then of course– unfortunately in some cases we’ve had this problem, people erase whatever the issue is. We try– do not do that. So, that first question is, 311/911. Second issue, when that happens, it’s obviously hurtful and horrible. People want to know what happens to their reports. Now, you obviously have a bias, you have a antisemitic. You don’t know exactly legally. But how can those who report hate crimes and even bias incidents under this two-tiered program now– obviously, we’re looking at hate graffiti traditionally, and how can they know the results of any investigatory process for a particular incident? How do they know what happened to their efforts?
Thank you very much for your question, Council Member.
Thank you.

So, when 911 or 311 are called, police respond to the scene, take the report, and the possible bias procedure is implemented, and obviously there’s a hate component. That case is then investigated actively by the Hate Crime Taskforce. Obviously, in an incident that you outlined that would be a swastika on real property, obviously a video canvas would be conducted, interviews would be conducted. Witness canvases would be conducted, and we’d extend those to look for the best possible prohibitive image of who committed such a crime. As the investigation progresses from inception to conclusion, obviously the custodian of that property would be contacted, and obviously there would be conversations including and not limited to the cost to clean that up, and you know, request for video footage if they were custodians of the video in that building. As the investigation progresses and if we were to make an arrest in that situation, they would be notified by the investigator from the Hate Crime Taskforce that it’s progressing with the investigation and affecting that arrest. Because for prosecutorial purposes, that deponent or custodian of the video or reporter whose building was defaced

would then have to proceed in the criminal justice system with the DA’s Office.

Then say for instance it was a passerby who noticed it, who did exactly what you suggested, 311/911, stayed on the scene. They wouldn't necessarily know because they don’t live in the building. They’re not the custodian, right?
Correct.

Is there some way we could have that information be available as time goes on so that they do know. I don’t know– it wouldn't be in every case, but that is the question that we get. What happens after I did what I felt was my civic duty?
I think it’s a fair point. I think– I think it’s a little bit complicated, right, when you’re talking about sharing information in an ongoing investigation.
No, I know. It would be the very end of the conclusion.

Yeah. Yeah. but I tell you what you’re saying, I think– it sounds like what you’re saying is or we should think about

for the case detective, right– certainly in a situation where an arrest has been made.
That’s– yes.
Right. Letting people know–
[interposing] Of course, like many cases, no arrests, many cases.
Right. But arrest or a no arrest, but basically the cases come to confusion.
Correct.

Hey, letting people know what happened and not thinking about it just in terms of the complainant, but also witnesses who– to your point, the witnesses who identified something, did the right thing, is invested and they want to hear. I think it’s a very fair point and we can definitely take that back.
I would appreciate that, because that is– again, people will feel better when they know that something happened. Obviously if it’s a horrific situation they’re going to get information.
Sure.

I’m talking about the swastika on the building. You know, it disappears. They don’t know if the person was arrest– you know, they don’t know what happened. So, yes, if we could figure out some way of tracking that that’s appropriate for your work, but also for the public, I think that would be terrific. I’d love to hear back on it.
Point very well taken.
Thank you very much.

That concludes the administration testimony for this hearing. I want to thank the NYPD, the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, and District Attorney Gonzalez for their testimony, for answering our questions today, and for being working partners to combat antisemitism here in our city. We will soon call the public session . As a reminder, if you’d like to testify in-person, you must fill out a slip with a Sergeant in the back of the room, and we will be calling those names shortly. Thank you.
We’re going to take a five-minute recess everyone, five-minute recess. Thank you. [break]

Thank you. Thank you for your patience. I would like to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding, and before you testify reminder that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public and spectators shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing recording. As a reminder, if you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today’s hearing topic: reporting on antisemitic hate crimes and bias incidents in New York City. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to

submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. I will now call the first panel. Ruth Lichtenstein, Hillary Stuchin, Brandon Pinsker, and Scott Richman. Reminder that when you testify, please state your name and if you’re with an organization, the organization for the record. We’ll go from my right to my life. So, Ruth, you’ll begin. Again, please state your name for the record. And a reminder, testimony is limited to two minutes. Thank you.

Okay. Ruth Lichtenstein, Project Witness, Holocaust Education Resource Center, Brooklyn, New York. Okay. So, let me introduct myself and what am I doing here. I think that it will be easier if I share with you one picture, and this is a picture of my– this is a picture of my half brother, one of million and a half children who were murdered in the Holocaust. He was murdered in Auschwitz four months before liberation. Saying that, I am a proud daughter of two Holocaust survivors. While my mother spoke, my father did not. Whatever he did not, he put in writing and I learned. From his silence, I learned. He left me a will, and in the will I just want to share with you two lines.

“We cannot correct these wrongs, but we can and must recount for those in the future who will come after us so our memories are not going to disappear into the abyss or forgotten.” Saying that, there is no need to explain today about the spread of antisemitism. We heard now for a long time a very, very, very important discussion about what could be done about hate crime. But I believe that having the experience with relationship with different organizations, if this is in New York State, if this is New York City, if this is across the United States, or if this is in Europe or in other location in the world. Antisemitism today, if we want to fight it, number one, number two, number three is education, and we need your help in order to move things the way that it should be. This is a must. This is something that we cannot rely anymore to what is going on in the public school system, and I am saying it as somebody who has long-experience–
[interposing] Yes. Thank you.
with the administration.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

Chair Vernikov, Chair Dinowitz, and members of the taskforce, thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the urgent matter of data and reporting of antisemitic incidents in New York City. My name is Scott Richman and I’m honored to serve as the Regional Director for ADL’s New York and New Jersey region. ADL is the leading anti-hate organization in the world, dedicated since 1913 to fighting against antisemitism and securing justice and fair treatment to all. A core part of the work of my team is tracking and responding to antisemitic incidents. From that we know firsthand that we face an alarming situation in New York City. Consistently, the city with more antisemitic incidents than any other city across the nation by far. This was the case before October 7th, 2023, and our most recent audit shows that number nearly tripled in the post 10/7 period. Data drives policy. These statistics are there for critical to countering antisemitism and hate, and yet, we know that they represent only part of the picture. Experts widely agree that hate

crimes and hate incidents are significantly under-reported. Barriers to reporting exist for many communities, particularly marginalized communities ranging from language barriers to fear of retaliation to a perception that authorities will not take the incident seriously or be able to respond. Compounding the problem is the fact that the NYPD statistics capture only criminal conduct. Yet, the vast majority of antisemitic acts to which we track and respond do not rise to the level of a crime. And while the New York City Commission on Human Rights does track discrimination complaints on the basis “creed” the data is not broken out based on religious affiliation. So we do not know how many of these incidents are actually anti-Jewish. To bridge the gaps, we strongly support Speaker Menin’s proposal to establish a dedicated hotline to report incidents to the New York City Commission on Human Rights, but this must include a breakdown by bias type to allow us to better resource the threat. We encourage this taskforce to consider additional avenues of data collection and information sharing between city agencies such as the New York City Public Schools. The establishment of this taskforce is an important

first step. Thank you for your leadership and the opportunity to testify.
Thank you.

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chairs Dinowitz and Vernikov, taskforce members. Thank you very much for convening this very important hearing. My name is Brandon Pinsker and I am the Acting Director of American Jewish Committees New York Regional Office, AJC New York. I also want to thank Commissioner Jessica Tisch for responding to concerns about the NYPD’s hate crimes reporting and for restoring and ensuring the publication of both reported incidents and confirmed cases. This was the right decision. These two data points serve different purposes. Reported incidents give us a real-time picture of what communities are experiencing. Confirmed cases reflect the legal standard after investigation. We need both to understand trends, respond early, and maintain public trust. Even with that correction, it’s important to be clear. Hate crimes data captures only part of what’s happening. Many incidents, as we know, are never reported. Others don’t meet the formal classification threshold. The numbers we discuss are

incomplete by definition. That’s why perception and behavior matters just as much as incident counts. According to AJC’s State of Antisemitism in America report released earlier this year in 2025, 56 percent of New York Jews have changed their behavior out of fear of antisemitism. That means avoiding Jewish synagogues and institutions, removing one’s yamikah or Star of David necklace. In 2021, that number was 36 percent. So, in the past four years we’ve seen a 20 percent increase in people fearing being Jewish and displaying that behavior. But it’s not just statistic. It’s how people move through the world, their daily lives here in New York City, the city with almost a million Jews. We need to be honest about where we are. Antisemitism is not just rising, it is becoming normalized. This is the line we cannot afford to ignore. On behalf of AJC, thank you, and we look forward to being constructive partners in the work ahead.

Hi. Thank you, Chairs Dinowitz, Vernikov, Council Member Brewer, for being here holding this hearing that is just of such importance to our community. I’m Hillary Stuchin. I’m Government Relations Director at UJA. Proud to

represent us today. So, first, we just want to appreciate the creation of this taskforce to begin with, to help address the issue of antisemitism in New York. We’re so happy that it is being recognized as such a major issue among this council. Because while we’ve seen a decrease in violent crime, we do know that antisemitism has only surged, and this must be addressed. We do recognize Commissioner Tisch for rolling back the NYPD hate and bias reporting changes. Limiting those reports to only confirmed hate crimes would have created a false sense of security while diminishing the transparency and representation of antisemitism in New York City. But we do know that hate crimes remain under-reported. And to achieve a better understanding of the range of incidents, we recommend and stand with many of our colleagues in this– in the following. So, the Council must urge the administration to increase reporting mechanisms and data sharing between city agencies so we can get a fuller picture of everything. The Commission of Human Rights should detail its data related to discrimination based on creed, as noted by ADL. Breaking out incidents by religion will help clarify threats against different

faith groups and provide a more complete picture again. Council should prioritize the implementation of Speaker’s proposal for a dedicated hotline at the Commission on Human Rights. And with the Jewish increasing under threat, we further encourage that the data collected include a breakdown by bias type to facilitate analysis. And finally, we also urge the city to increase educational resources and victim support in communities that are underserved. It’s critical that the Jewish community and actually all communities across New York City feel safe, protected, and supported. We look forward to partnering with the taskforce in its efforts to address these issues. Thank you.

Thank you. And I encourage us to continue the conversation, because as you were hearing during the committee and as you are testifying, there’s a lot of room for data sharing, a lot of room to improve reporting, whether it’s through the DA’s Office and the NYPD or the Commission of Human Rights, disaggregating certain data would certainly be helpful. And we look forward to continuing these conversations with you about ways to increase transparency and data sharing, data

reporting to address this really serious crisis in our city. Thank you so much for your testimony.
Thank you for being here. I’ll call the next panel. Gerard Filitti, Alan Scheiner, Avrohom Malachowski, and Mosche Spern.

Good afternoon. Thank you, Chair Vernikov, Chair Dinowitz and the taskforce, for this opportunity to speak. My name is Gerard Filitti. I’m a Civil Rights Attorney and Senior Counsel at the Lawfare Project, as well as Counsel for the End Jew Hatred Civil Rights Group where I work on a daily basis with victims of hate crime including in New York City. From what I’ve seen over the last many years, there is a significant disparity in how Jewish victims are treated under the law, and the consequences that are imposed on their attackers, and this is a major problem. The biggest deterrent that we see is when consequences are imposed on acts of hate targeting a minority community, and we’re just not seeing that in New York City. It seems to be a structural problem between NYPD and some of the DA’s offices, and that’s best highlighted by the number of cases that have been

taken on by the Federal Justice Department when DA Alvin Bragg or other District Attorneys have not actually moved forward with prosecutions on clear cuts act of violence against Jews. This is also an issue that we’ve seen with NYPD where there seems to be some misunderstanding or intentional misreading of laws that do not give them the best ability to pursue charges in instances that should be very clear cut as we saw at Park East Synagogue, again, requiring the federal government to step in. So, I would ask that this taskforce and the City Council work closely to figure out and impose more clarity and more transparency on how the NYPD and the District Attorney’s offices are actually handling these hate crimes in reality, because the testimony that we often hear from their officials seems to be that they’re doing everything they can when that in my experience as an attorney working with hate crime victims is simply not the case.
Thank you.

Good afternoon. I’m Alan Scheiner. I’m the Senior Litigation Counsel at the National Jewish Advocacy Center. We’re a nonprofit law firm litigating against antisemitic

discrimination, violence and terrorism. NYPD data shows that on average Jewish New Yorkers are the victim of hate crimes nearly every day, six out of seven days per week. More broadly, recent weeks have seen bomb and gun attacks on synagogues in the UK and Canada, and in March in Michigan a Jewish synagogue and preschool was attacked by a gunman driving a car bomb that could have killed dozens of children. One result of the campaign of violence against Jews is fear, fear that I’ve seen in my daily work at NJAC. Many Jews are afraid to publicly identify as Jewish or to speak up in defense of Jewish rights in their workplace or at a school or on social media or in public spaces. Although the Mayor has acknowledged the hate crime statistics, his response does not match the data. The city has shown indifference to the heightened particular peril faced by Jewish New Yorkers, and that indifference reflects bias and threatens Jewish safety and Jewish lives. Among many other things, the NYPD stood by as two synagogues were besieged by mobs threatening harm, engaged in menacing and harassment. If the NYPD believes that to yell threats at Jews within sight and sound of worshipers is protected First Amendment activity and

lawful, they are mistaken about the law. The Mayor has not yet signed the City Council’s very modest legislation calling for reporting on the protection of houses of worship. I want to note also today is Yom Ha’atzmaut, Israel’s Independence Day, celebrating the declaration and legal recognition of the state of Israel 78 years ago. Today, my office received reliable reports of Jewish schools in the United States being closed due to bomb threats. That is not a coincidence. Many like to pretend that crimes motivated by hatred of Israel are not antisemitic, but that is a grave error. Anti-zionism is the most common species of antisemitism today.
Thank you. Go ahead.

Chair Vernikov, Chair Dinowitz, my name is Avrohom Malachowski. I am here representing the Auschwitz Jewish Center Foundation. We come first to express our appreciation. Speaker Menin’s decision to establish the taskforce was not symbolic. It was necessary. Antisemitism is New York City is not abstract. It is measurable, visible and to too many in our community, lived. The data is clear. The incidents are real.

The impact has been profound on students, families and institutions across our city. The taskforce sends an important signal, that the Council recognizes both the scale of the issue and the responsibility to confront it. That matters. The Auschwitz Jewish Center Foundation has been proud to partner with this council in that effort. Through our Decode Hate program, together, we are currently reaching nearly 30,000 middle and high school students throughout New York City’s public schools this academic year, providing them with the tools to recognize, understand and confront antisemitism and hate in the environment where it lives increasingly online. That work is ongoing. It is structured, and it is delivering results. But education alone is not enough. Addressing antisemitism requires enforcement, accountability and sustained institutional leadership. That is the role this taskforce has been thankfully employed to play. We are here today to say clearly we stand with you and we’re ready to support you in that work. We view this body not only as necessary, but essential to ensuring that the response to antisemitism in the city is coordinated, serious, and sustained. We look forward

to working with you, this body, and helping wherever it is possible to ensure your success. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Mr. Spern?

Hi, Moshe Spern. I’m an educator and Jewish community advocate, and I sit here before you, Councilwoman Vernikov, Councilman Dinowitz, as someone who personally experienced antisemitism right before October 7th. I’m an educator teaching a classroom when a student stood up and for the first time in my career had done something antisemitic to me by doing a gesture of a hail Hitler. And that in itself was very, very, very traumatic. A week later, October 7th happened, and of course, as you both know, that sort of opened up my advocacy. My principal did nothing wrong, reported it to the right places, did everything right, consulted with me, investigated, and everything was done by the book. But I know this, because when I reported this incident to the Adams administration, the Borough Safety Director of Queens reached out to my principal. My principal was quite surprised. He didn’t know that I had reported this,

and he wanted to make sure he did everything right. He was told he did. But I was never interviewed by NYPD. there was never any followup from anyone in the Superintendent or DOE office. In the last couple years, for the first time in a school that I’ve been in for over 12 years, we’ve had multiple swastikas in our school. And it’s not just– as you both know, people come to be about other– about antisemitism in their schools. This was the first time I was dealing with it in my own school, one in which I discovered– that a student had shown me– and we had– I shared it with the administration. NYPD was called in. I was interviewed a couple times. The point that I’m making is, when I found out other schools within my superintendency was dealing with the same issue, I reached out to my superintendent who then directed me that he was taking guidance from the meeting the moment in the chancellor’s office of New York City schools. When I reached out to them, I got silence. That continues to happen in New York City public schools. When you report things to the people on top, there was silence. There is no help. As we both know with Sammy Steichman [sp?], who was denied speaking in a school initially. When I reached out,

this actually would not have ever hit the media had I been responded to by the superintendent of that district. The point is, the people in power never listen.

Thank you, Mr. Spern. I just have one question for Mr. Filitti. Mr. Filitti, as a Civil Rights attorney, after listening to the testify from city agencies this afternoon and the NYPD, do you– and the DA’s offices. Do you believe they are limited in their ability to investigate and prosecute hate crimes?

I think that they’re all limited by the lack or presence of political will. I’ll give you two examples. One is the application of penal code 240.-- [inaudible] need my glasses for this– 240.21 which you read verbatim into the record, and 240.70 which is also New York penal code about protests at synagogues and house of worship. Now, when we say the Park East protest directly targeting it meant to intimate people who were attending religious service at Park East Synagogue. Those could have been pursued as criminal charges by NYPD. They were not. There’s never been a clear explanation given as to why they were not. Instead, they’re

leaving it to the federal government to come into what is essentially a city prosecution a state law case. And the other example that really strikes a nerve is the example of zionist written on a– graffiti’d onto a restaurant that is– that has kosher food. The problem there is that this is not a question. This is not an open-ended question. This is a question that should be resolved in favor of the finding of an attempt to commit a crime on the basis of either religion, ancestry or national origin, because when you have that combination of a kosher restaurant and zionists which is understood by most to be a component of Jewish identity, that is something that should be de facto and primarily identified as a potential hate crime and investigated as such. The fact that we’re not seeing NYPD provide clear answers, leads the question as to whether they actually have guidance. And I encourage this taskforce to get those answers in the sense of what guidance NYPD has, what materials they use in order to make these determinations and how they come to them, because as a matter of law, a lot of these determinations are questionable and probably wrong.

Thank you very much. Thank you for your testimony, your expertise, sharing it [inaudible] with us and sharing your experiences. We will definitely do our very best to follow up to hold individuals accountable and to take action. Thank you. This panel is excused. And now we will call the next panel: Jack Lster, Carin Feldman, Abe Postnik [sp?], Moshe Davis, and Leo Ferguson. You can begin.

Hello, Chairs Dinowitz and Chair Vernikov and Council Members. My name is Leo Fergusson. I am the Scholar and Resident of Jews for Racial and Economic Justice on behalf of whom I’m testifying. I’m not going to repeat the statistics. We all agree that hate crimes are rising and that even one is too many. The only real question is, what are we going to do about it? At the outset of this hearing, Chair Dinowitz said we will not be the government of inaction, but that’s largely what we’ve had for as long as I’ve been doing this work. I have been to many hearings like this one. I hve heard a lot of zero tolerance rhetoric. I’ve heard the NYPD testify over and over again about all the things that they are doing, and that entire time I have just

watched the numbers go up and up and up. We don’t get any actual, real, effective policy. New Yorkers deserve to have hate violence taken seriously and deserve policy solutions that make them safer. It is difficult to understand how we’re going to get real effective policy when unfortunately – very unfortunately you have a co-chair of this committee who has spouted an ongoing litany of bigoted and egregious statements directed at Muslims, about queer New Yorkers and even about other Jews. that Council Member Vernikov is the co-chair of a committee that is ostensibly dedicated to fighting hate undermines the credibility of this committee and make it hard to see it as anything an attempt to separate and alienate Jews from the rest of New York, something that can only serve the interest of antisemites. There is no safety for New York’s Jewish community that does not include a safety and respect for all New York’s communities. Since our mayor has been giving us a masterclass on what Democratic Socialism can accomplish for the City, it’s with remembering that antisemitism has famously been called the socialism of fools. While substituting empty publicity stunts and rhetoric for good evidence-based

policy is the hate violence prevention of pools [sic]. I have unfortunately watched the co-chairs here demonstrate their ignorance of even the most basic facts about how hate crimes are charged. I haven’t heard a single work about any kind of serious rigorous policy response that would serve the one million Jews who live in the city. This is not a serious committee, and unfortunately I don’t think the co-chairs are serious people. New York’s Jewish community deserves much better.
Thank you. Go ahead.

Hi. My name is Karen Feldman and I am a veteran New York City public school teacher, educational coordinator at the Govera [sp?] Fund and co-founder of the New York city Public School Alliance. For nearly a decade, I have documented antisemitism in our public schools, something students, educators and families are now confronting every day. I recognize this hearing is not a focus specifically on education, but I’m here to share what I’ve witnessed firsthand, both in the classroom and through my work with the New York City Public School Alliance. I also want to acknowledge

the New York City Public School Alliance’s joint report with NCRI, Entryism, the Rise of Antisemitism, Anti-Israel, and Anti-American bias in the New York City schools. The reflection they reflect– sorry– it reflects and defines what we are seeing across the system. Antisemitism among the youth is rising at an alarming rate. It is becoming embedded in school environments, often goes under-reported and it is not being addressed with the seriousness it demands. For example, a student at Wagner High School in Staten Island was repeatedly called a dirty Jew. He reported the incident, completed the proper documentation, trusting it would be handled appropriately in school. Instead, the report was misfiled as a non-bias incident, and it never received the investigation it warranted. Therefore, he reached out to me for guidance and help. As Rabbi Johnathan Sachs [sp?], a blessed memory warned, antisemitism is a mutating virus. Today we are seeing that mutation as anti-zionism, often disguised as social justice. Since October 7th, 2023, the New York City Public School Alliance has collected over 11,000 pieces of evidence. The patterns are consistent, widespread and deeply concerning. Jewish students report being

called slurs such as Jew dog, baby killers. In addition, being accused of– I’m happy to provide the needed documentation for future hearings from these reports.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Vernikov and Chair Dinowitz. Thank you for convening this important hearing and thank you for Speaker Menin for your leadership in establishing this taskforce. Sure. Thank you, Chair. Understand and apply the IHRA definition correctly, you have to understand both what I was explaining about Jewish peoplehood, but you also have to understand that the way antisemitism manifests throughout the centuries is that it villainizes the Jews. It demonizes the Jews, right? The Jews become

the source of the evil. Jews are often– and this is what the IHRA definition explicitly states– is that Jews are frequently blamed for why things go wrong or accused of trying to harm humanity. And then the way it progresses is the idea is well, since the Jews are standing between us and utopia, we need to push the Jews out of acceptable society. What we see today and what the IHRA definition explains is that Israel is frequently treated as the “Jewish collective" as the collective Jew. So, if antisemitism is targeting not only individual Jews, but the Jewish people, sometimes what happens is you get people who will just substitute in the world Israel, when what they’re really referring to is the Jewish people. That’s not a criticism of the policies of the government of Israel which the IHRA definition explicitly states cannot be regarded as antisemitic. That’s antisemitism, and that’s how the IHRA definition– it doesn’t conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism.
